name: Gareth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of four full-time workers at Carrow Hill, which is about four hundred hectares of wheat, oilseed and beans, plus a pig unit with six hundred sows. The farm is owned by a farming company with three other sites, and I mostly do the tractor work and help in the pig unit when they're short. Today was drilling winter beans, then I went over to the farrowing house, where the sows give birth, because a lad was off sick. I love the machinery and I love fiddling with new kit, what wears me out is that the pay's not moved in years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: When you say you like fiddling with new kit, what does that look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the one who set up the drone that flies over the wheat and spots the patches that need more fertiliser. I talk to an AI assistant on my phone every day, about everything, from a rattle in the drill to what a sow's off-colour skin might mean before I ring the vet. The manager calls me ‘the professor’, which is a joke because I've only got my agricultural certificate from college. Money is the weak spot, we rent our house in the village and after the car and the bills there's maybe two or three weeks' worth left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, it was useful and it could have done more. I'd post in the farming tech group I'm in that people gave up on it too soon. And down the pub I'd be the one defending it while everyone else laughed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd be no change, really, which is fine but a bit flat. I'd still use the tools every day because they help me. The things that bother me are my pay and the company's attitude to the workers, and AI was never going to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. Keep the drone going, keep using the assistant, maybe push the manager to let me trial a weed-spotting camera on the sprayer. And I'd keep nagging the company for a pay review, the same as every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A touch let down, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit like when the electric car you wanted turns out to need charging every forty miles. You still drive it, you just stop telling people about it. Yes, disappointed, but I'd get over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your days be any different in eight years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same yard, same tractor, sore back. I'd be sixty-six and thinking about the state pension. I'd like to be still useful to someone, mending drones for the neighbours maybe.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame, because it was useful and could have done more. I'd post in my farming tech group that people gave up too soon.
S0.think: For me it'd be no change, which is fine but flat. My real complaints are the pay and how the company treats workers, which AI was never going to fix.
S0.do: Keeps running the farm's drone and using an AI assistant daily. Pushes the manager to trial a weed-spotting camera and asks the company for a pay review again.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of disappointment.
S0.quote: A bit like when the electric car you wanted turns out to need charging every forty miles.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is a natural tinkerer and would be a little disappointed by a plateau rather than relieved. His frustration is with pay and the company, not technology. He sees his future usefulness in fixing and running new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's turn the dial up a bit. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bring it on, but share the gains. If a robot weeder saves the company a person's wages, then some of that should go to the people still there and to training the ones moving on. I'd say that online and I'd say it to the area manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd do quite well out of it. I'm already the one who knows the drone and the software, so I'd be the one they'd put in charge of any robots. That's not a nice thought when the others are less sure, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to send me on the manufacturer's course for whatever robot they buy, in the first six months. I'd offer to run the trial on one field before they buy a fleet. And I'd start a small side thing setting up drones for smaller farms nearby, weekends only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited, a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want the robots. But what if they replace one of the four workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the guilty bit. Kev's been on that farm longer than me and he can't text with both thumbs, and I know who they'd keep. I'd try to get Kev on the course with me, but I can't make him learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the company for more money if you're the one running the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask, yes, and I'd ask for Kev too. The company should pay people properly when the job changes. I'd probably get a bit more and Kev would get a pat on the back, if I'm honest.

S1.say: I'd say bring it on, but share the gains. If a robot weeder saves a wage, part of that should go to the remaining staff and to training those who leave.
S1.think: I think I'd do quite well, because I already run the drone and software and would be put in charge of the robots. That's uncomfortable when others are less sure.
S1.do: Asks the company to send him on the robot maker's training course within six months and offers to run a one-field trial. Starts a weekend side business setting up drones for smaller farms.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about colleagues.
S1.quote: Kev's been on that farm longer than me and he can't text with both thumbs, and I know who they'd keep.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth expects to gain from steady change, and his guilt about Kev is real and specific. He wants the gains shared and would push for co-workers, but he's honest that the company would keep him over Kev. His side business plan shows how quickly he'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and it needs public control. The machines should be owned partly by the public or by the workers, not just a few companies. I'd say that in the tech group and they'd probably shout me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not the robots that scare me, it's the speed. For a year or two the company would need someone like me to babysit the machines, then not. And I'd be sixty with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd learn every robot on the market, using the AI assistant to cram. I'd go to the company with a plan: let me run the robots across all four sites. Then I'd set up as a contractor servicing robots on smaller farms, because they'll need help and can't afford the dealer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but anxious. There's excitement in it too, which I'm almost embarrassed to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With no savings to speak of, what's your fallback if the company lets you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Contract work on other farms, and Sian's job, she's a home care worker. And the state, honestly, if it comes to it. I'm all for a basic income, I've argued for it for years, I just never thought I'd be first in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farm would need a minder. How long do you think that job lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year, two at most, until the robots can fix the robots. That's the bit I keep coming back to. I'd be racing a machine that learns faster than me, and with two years' notice I'd lose.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and needs public control: machines should be owned partly by the public or the workers. My tech group would probably shout me down.
S2.think: It's the speed that scares me, not the robots. The company would need someone to babysit the machines for a year or two, then not, and I'd be sixty with no savings.
S2.do: Crams on every robot on the market using an AI assistant and pitches running robots across all four company sites. Sets up as a contractor servicing robots on smaller farms.
S2.feel: Anxious and embarrassed to also feel some excitement.
S2.quote: I'm all for a basic income, I've argued for it for years, I just never thought I'd be first in the queue.
S2.fieldNote: Even under fast AGI Gareth moves first, but he sees clearly that his edge would expire. His long-held support for a basic income becomes personal, which he notes with dry humour. Thin savings and his age keep the worry real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with a little more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set it up fairly, so let's not waste them. Unions, councils, farmers, all at the same table. I'd be posting about it, and I'd go to the union branch for the first time in years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to become the go-to robot person in the area before the robots don't need anyone. I'd be sixty-three, and with luck that carries me nearly to pension age. It's tighter than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper course in farm robotics, evenings, and try to get the company to pay. I'd build up the drone and robot servicing business on weekends, so it's ready when the farm doesn't need me. And I'd join the union again, because I'd want a voice in how the company handles it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. With five years, I think I can ride it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings, small as they are, in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put every bit of side money into savings, not the business, honestly. The worst thing would be spending my last spare pound on a robot that's cheaper next year. I'd buy tools, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to the other workers about any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd set up a group chat for the four of us and the other sites, and drag Kev into it. I'd want us asking the company together what the plan is, not each going in alone.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to do it fairly, so unions, councils and farmers should sit at the same table. I'd post about it and go back to the union branch.
S3.think: Five years lets me become the area's robot person before robots stop needing people. At sixty-three that nearly gets me to pension age, but it's tight.
S3.do: Takes an evening course in farm robotics and asks the company to pay for it. Builds a weekend servicing business, saves side income instead of buying machines, and rejoins the union with his co-workers.
S3.feel: Uneasy but fairly confident he can ride it out.
S3.quote: The worst thing would be spending my last spare pound on a robot that's cheaper next year.
S3.fieldNote: Five years changes his strategy from a scramble into a plan, and he's sharp about not buying machines that will be cheaper next year. He wants to organise his co-workers, which ties his progressive views to action. Rejoining the union is new and telling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get this right, so there's no excuse. Training funds, shared ownership of machines, a decent pension. I'd be pushing that online and with the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally ten years is fine. I'd use the decade to build skills and a bit of a business and then retire as it arrives. I think I'd quite enjoy watching it, in a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn robotics properly and keep using AI every day, which I do anyway. I'd grow the side business slowly and hand it to a younger lad from the village by 2034. And I'd keep working at Carrow Hill as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-eight in 2036. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be the old boy sitting on the gate explaining to the robot why the bottom field floods. Probably helping my grandkids with their homework, which will be done by AI anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sian. Care work is going to be one of the last things robots do well, but it'll still change. And the lads I work with. Kev retires in about three years, so he's fine, but the young ones aren't.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse: training funds, shared ownership of machines and a decent pension. I'd push for it online and with the union.
S4.think: Ten years is fine for me personally; I'd build skills and a small business, then retire as it arrives. I'd quite enjoy watching it.
S4.do: Learns robotics properly and keeps using AI daily while staying in his farm job. Grows his side business slowly and plans to hand it to a younger person from the village by 2034.
S4.quote: I'd be the old boy sitting on the gate explaining to the robot why the bottom field floods.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Gareth is relaxed and almost enjoys the prospect. His concern shifts to his partner's care work and the young workers. He is the rare person here who'd plan a handover of something he hasn't built yet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's not the robots I'm scared of, it's being sixty with no savings and no time to turn round. What would help is a proper basic income and some public ownership of the machines, so the money from them doesn't just leave the village.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people like me actually get listened to. I've had ideas about that farm for years and nobody upstairs asks. If the robots come, I'd want the workers to have a say in how, not just be told.

headlineQuote: It's not the robots I'm scared of, it's being sixty with no savings and no time to turn round.
portrait: Gareth Jensen is a 58-year-old farm worker who drives tractors and helps in the pig unit on a company-owned farm, renting a house in the village with very little saved. He uses an AI assistant every day, runs the farm's drone and loves new kit. He leans left and wants the gains from machines shared with workers. He is calm about a plateau and about steady change, where he expects to run the robots, but anxious about AGI in 2028 because his edge would expire before his pension. With five or ten years he plans courses, a weekend robot-servicing business and organising his co-workers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be sixty with no savings and no time to turn round.
whatWouldHelp: A proper basic income and some public ownership of the machines, so the money they make stays in the village.
